source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade, Persson (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (read via Clearing House Unterricht summary SR 18)
finding: Critical thinking can be taught in class. The overall effect is small to medium and stable across school level, subject and length of intervention.
numbers: Overall g = 0.30 over 341 effects from the higher-quality studies (867 English studies 1930-2009 screened). About 60% chance a treated student beats a control. Significant even for interventions of 1 hour to 2 days.
limits: Read the secondary summary, not the journal paper (paywalled). Summary says '341 studies'; the Stanford Encyclopedia says 341 effect sizes. Mostly English-language, pre-2010. Design and test type moderated results, so weak studies were removed first.
agent_relevance: A base rate: one instructional lever is worth about 0.3 SD. Do not expect large gains from one prompt trick.

source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade, Persson (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (read via Clearing House Unterricht summary SR 18)
finding: The gain depends on the outcome. Content-specific critical thinking improved most; dispositions least.
numbers: Content-specific CT g = 0.57 (97 studies). Dispositions g = 0.23 (25 studies). Subject fact learning g = 0.33 (140 studies). Generic CT g = 0.30.
limits: Content-specific tests sit close to what was taught, so the big number partly reflects near transfer.
agent_relevance: Score our checks on in-domain tasks; expect smaller gain on unseen task types.

source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade, Persson (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (read via Clearing House Unterricht summary SR 18)
finding: Three promotion strategies each help alone, and the combination helps most: authentic or anchored instruction, dialogue, mentoring.
numbers: All three combined g = 0.57 (19 studies), medium. Each strategy alone significant.
limits: Only 19 studies in the combined cell. Strategies are confounded in real programs, so this is not causal proof of an interaction.
agent_relevance: Agent analogues: authentic task with real feedback; dialogue as isolated attempts exchanging only evidence; mentoring as retrieved lessons or solved cases. Combine rather than pick one.

source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade, Persson (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (read via Clearing House Unterricht summary SR 18)
finding: Specific variants worked: teacher questioning, whole-class and small-group discussion, problem solving, role play.
numbers: Dialogue: teacher questions g = 0.38 (19 studies); whole-class guided discussion g = 0.42 (16); small-group g = 0.41 (14). Authentic/anchored: problem solving g = 0.35 (31); role play g = 0.61 (5).
limits: Role play rests on 5 studies. Differences between variants not claimed significant.
agent_relevance: Questioning and discussion have similar value; a structure that forces a reply to a challenge is a plausible lever.

source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade, Persson (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (read via Clearing House Unterricht summary SR 18)
finding: Delivery mode (stand-alone CT lessons vs infused in content) did not differ much. The best form taught abstract principles explicitly, then applied them to concrete content.
numbers: No significant difference explicit vs infused. Explicit-principles-then-applied was most effective (exact g not in the summary).
limits: Exact moderator values are in the original handout, not read.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the agent both a general rule (guardrail) and a worked application.

source: Abrami, Bernard, Borokhovski, Waddington, Wade, Persson (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis (read via Clearing House Unterricht summary SR 18)
finding: Age and subject did not significantly change the effect.
numbers: Ages 11-15 g = 0.37 vs 16-18 g = 0.25 (not significant). STEM vs non-STEM no significant difference.
limits: No analysis by country or era. Short interventions risk teaching to the test.
agent_relevance: The effect is not tied to one domain, but this says nothing about transfer to novel domains.

source: Hitchcock, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Critical Thinking: Educational Methods supplement
finding: Describes the Abrami 2015 inclusion rules and says explicit CT instruction can improve abilities and dispositions on standardized tests.
numbers: Weighted mean effect 0.30 over 341 effect sizes, range -1 to +2. Inclusion: intervention of at least 3 hours, a control group, a standardized test (Watson-Glaser, Cornell, CCTST, CCTDI). Single-group pre-post studies dropped.
quote: This methodologically careful meta-analysis provides strong statistical evidence that explicit instruction for critical thinking can improve
limits: Few true randomized experiments because classrooms rarely randomize. The -1 to +2 spread shows some instruction hurts.
agent_relevance: Measure each lever instead of assuming it helps.

source: Huber & Kuncel (2016) Does college teach critical thinking? A meta-analysis (read AERA snapshot and Crossref abstract)
finding: Critical thinking skills and dispositions rise a lot over a normal college. Programs aimed at general CT did not add long-term gains beyond that.
numbers: 71 research reports over 48 years. About the 50th to 72nd percentile over four years. Nursing students (CT-emphasizing) did not gain more than others.
limits: Snapshot gives no exact effect sizes. Mostly pre/post gains, so maturation and subject learning are mixed in.
agent_relevance: Special CT training may add little over ordinary content learning; our scaffold must beat strong plain baselines, not weak ones.

source: Meta-analysis of non-traditional teaching on critical thinking of nursing students (PMC5025580)
finding: Non-lecture methods raised CT dispositions and skills in nursing students.
numbers: Dispositions (CCTDI, 8 datasets) SMD 0.42, 95% CI 0.26-0.57. Skills (CCTST, 6 datasets) SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.10-0.48. Studies 2001-2014.
limits: Few datasets; moderate to high heterogeneity; weak blinding and concealment; PBL evidence called insufficient. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: Skills gain about 0.3 matches Abrami: active methods give a stable but modest gain.

source: Insight Assessment (2023) Teaching for Critical Thinking handout
finding: Practitioner advice derived from Abrami: teach through active tasks, name the reasoning skills, wait 10-15 seconds after questions, give frequent practice and formative feedback.
numbers: No new data. Cites Abrami 2015 and Abrami 2008 stage-one meta-analysis.
limits: Vendor of CT tests; the wait-time claim has no source in the handout.
agent_relevance: Formative feedback tied to named reasoning moves matches our rule: revise only from real output.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models
finding: Showing a model worked solutions with steps raises accuracy on multi-step problems. This is the LLM version of the worked-example effect.
numbers: PaLM 540B, 8 exemplars: GSM8K 17.9 to 56.9 (+39.0); SVAMP 69.4 to 79.0; ASDiv 72.1 to 73.9; AQuA 25.2 to 35.8; MAWPS 79.2 to 93.3. Single-step problems: gains negative or very small.
limits: Gain appears only at large scale. Shown steps may not reflect how the model really decided.
agent_relevance: Retrieved solved examples with steps are well backed, but only for multi-step tasks.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models (ablations)
finding: The benefit comes from natural-language steps before the answer, not from extra compute alone or from the equation alone.
numbers: Three ablations tested: equation only, variable compute only, reasoning after answer. The text reports they do not match full chain of thought on GSM8K.
limits: Exact ablation numbers were in a figure and not read.
agent_relevance: Order matters: reasoning shown before the answer, as in worked examples.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: Several model instances propose answers, read each other and revise over rounds. This dialogue method beats single answers, reflection and majority vote.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. Biographies: 66.0, 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, debate 71.1. Chess validity: 29.3, 38.8, debate 45.2.
limits: Same base model for every agent, so errors are correlated (our G4). Reflection lowered GSM8K and MMLU. Gains flat beyond 4 rounds. Cost multiplies by agents and rounds; equal-compute comparison with majority vote not made at scale.
agent_relevance: Dialogue helps, but debate is read-and-persuade; our schema uses isolated attempts plus code selection. Compare at equal cost before adopting.

source: Du et al. (2023) multiagent debate, extra analyses
finding: Persona diversity gave a small extra gain; more agents and rounds help up to a plateau.
numbers: MMLU 71.1 to 74.2 when agents act as different personas (professor, doctor, mathematician). No gain beyond 4 rounds.
limits: Persona gain on one dataset only; conflicts with our G4 (no persona voters).
agent_relevance: Test personas ourselves; do not assume.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning, Scientific Reports
finding: A GPT-4 tutor built on pedagogy (step by step, scaffolds, self-paced, expert-written prompts with solutions) beat in-class active learning in a crossover RCT.
numbers: Harvard physics, N=194, two lessons crossover. Median post-score 4.5 (AI, N=142) vs 3.5 (active class, N=174); median gain over double; Mann-Whitney z=-5.6, p<1e-8. Regression effect 0.63 SD; quantile estimate 0.73 to 1.3 SD. Median time on task 49 min vs 60.
limits: Ceiling effect on post-test; first exposure to material (Bloom understand/apply/analyze); strong instructor-written prompts; authors say it may not hold for complex synthesis and higher-order critical thinking. Immediate post-test only.
agent_relevance: A tutor following known instruction principles wins. Problem-specific hand-written guidance beat generic. Supports lessons and worked solutions in the scaffold.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning, Scientific Reports
finding: Students felt more engaged and motivated with the AI tutor. Time on task did not predict post-test score.
numbers: Motivation higher, t(311)=-3.4, p<0.001. 70% of AI group spent under 60 min. 83% said tutor explanations were accurate.
limits: Self-report; novelty effect not controlled.
agent_relevance: Time spent is not the lever; structure is.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS
finding: Free GPT-4 access raised practice scores but lowered later unassisted scores. A tutor version with hints and the solution in the prompt removed the harm.
numbers: Field experiment, nearly 1000 high school students. Practice: GPT Base +0.137, GPT Tutor +0.361 (control mean 0.284), i.e. +48% and +127%. Unassisted exam: GPT Base -0.054 (about -17%, p<.05), GPT Tutor -0.004 (not significant).
limits: Randomized by classroom; honors classes excluded. A PNAS correction was published 2025-08-20 (content not read). The Tutor arm still did not beat control on the exam.
agent_relevance: Instruction that gives hints and withholds answers protects skill. Dinucu-Jianu shows the same trade-off in LLM tutors.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS
finding: Students overestimated their learning. GPT Base students did not notice they did worse; GPT Tutor students thought they did better than they did.
numbers: Self-rated learning exceeded measured learning in both AI arms. GPT Base often gave wrong answers (hallucination); the Tutor prompt included the solution.
limits: Self-report items; one setting.
agent_relevance: An agent's own confidence about its learning or answer is unreliable; use external checks.

source: Dinucu-Jianu, Macina, Daheim, Hakimi, Gurevych, Sachan (2025) From problem-solving to teaching problem-solving: aligning LLMs with pedagogy using reinforcement learning
finding: Standard LLMs are tuned to answer, not teach, and leak solutions. RL with a leakage penalty trades student gain against answer-giving; a 7B model matches LearnLM on pedagogy.
numbers: Simulated student-tutor dialogs (max 16 turns). Qwen2.5-72B and DeepSeek-V3 gave the highest solve-rate gains and high solution leakage. Penalty 0 gives max solve rate but leaks; penalty 0.75 balanced. SocraticLM and SFT lowered MMLU/GSM8K/MATH500 more than the RL models.
limits: Students are LLM-simulated and leakage is LLM-judged; no human learners. Exact table values not copied.
agent_relevance: Withholding the answer costs short-term solve rate; the answer-giving versus guiding balance must be set on purpose.

source: Barbieri et al. (2023) A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance, Educational Psychology Review
finding: Worked examples help mathematics performance at a medium size. Correct examples beat incorrect ones; adding self-explanation prompts did worse than examples alone.
numbers: 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes from 8033 abstracts. Average g = 0.48 (p=0.01, robust variance estimation). Effect held for practice and for initial skill acquisition.
limits: Read the abstract and preview only. Mathematics only. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: Use correct solved examples; do not assume extra 'reflect' prompts add value. Matches G1.

source: Sweller & Cooper (1985) The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra
finding: Founding worked-example experiments: studying solved algebra examples gave faster learning than solving problems alone (from memory; not opened).
numbers: Exact times and error counts not verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Expertise-reversal limit (examples help novices, not experts) is from later work and not verified here.
agent_relevance: Use examples early and drop them when the agent already solves the task.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: Argues unguided discovery is less effective than guided instruction for novices (from memory; not opened).
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Contested by inquiry-learning researchers. Compare Kestin 2025, where guided tutoring won.
agent_relevance: Guided steps beat open exploration on new problem types.

source: Abrami et al. (2008) Instructional interventions affecting critical thinking skills and dispositions: a stage 1 meta-analysis, Review of Educational Research 78, 1102-1134
finding: Earlier stage-one version of the 2015 work; the Insight handout cites it for the claim that programs that explicitly target CT outperform programs that only talk about it.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; known only from a citation in the Insight handout.
agent_relevance: Source for the claim that explicit targeting beats mere mention.

source: Du et al. (2023) multiagent debate, self-reflection baseline
finding: Asking one model to reflect on its own answer helped on arithmetic but hurt on GSM8K and MMLU. Self-critique is not reliable instruction.
numbers: Reflection vs single: arithmetic 72.1 vs 67.0; GSM8K 75.0 vs 77.0; MMLU 57.7 vs 63.9; chess validity 38.8 vs 29.3.
limits: Same model, one prompt style; small question sets.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: no self-review without real output.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) design note: what made the tutor work
finding: The authors credit expert-written, question-specific prompts, sequential guidance through each part of a problem, self-pacing and accurate explanations. They did not test which part matters.
numbers: No ablation. 83% of students rated tutor explanations accurate.
limits: Bundled design; cannot tell which component caused the 0.63 to 1.3 SD gain.
agent_relevance: Do not credit any one component; ablate each lever in our own scaffold.
